Chapter 2: Why God’s Glory and Human Happiness Belong Together
Picture this: you’re at a celebration with friends and family. There’s laughter all around, delicious food, and that warm feeling of belonging. But then, in the middle of it all, someone pauses and wonders—why do these moments of happiness slip away so quickly? The joy is real, but it never seems to stick around. Before long, life drifts back to the ordinary, and there’s this quiet longing for something more.
Most people, if we’re honest, spend their lives chasing happiness. We try to grab hold of it through success, comfort, or recognition. The world is full of promises, but none of them really fill us up. Even folks who are devoted to their faith can fall into the trap of thinking of God as just another way to get what they want. But you know how that ends—there’s always a sense of emptiness left behind.
Here’s something to pay attention to: God’s glory and our happiness aren’t two separate things. They’re actually deeply connected. When we find our deepest joy in God, that’s what truly honors Him. It’s kind of like a child who just lights up being with a loving parent—not because of the gifts or the treats, but because of who the parent is. When that joy is real, the parent’s heart is overflowing.
Think about a teacher who’s spent years trying to motivate students with rules and rewards. Sometimes it works, sometimes it totally backfires, but rarely does it spark real excitement. Then one day, the teacher shifts focus—not on the rules, but on the joy of learning itself. All of a sudden, the classroom comes alive. The students’ enthusiasm becomes the best reward, and the teacher finds real satisfaction as the kids thrive.
In the same way, God isn’t honored by reluctant obedience or half-hearted worship. What delights Him most is when we actually find pleasure in Him. That changes everything about how we live out our faith. God isn’t some taskmaster—we start to see Him as the source of everything good and beautiful. Chasing happiness isn’t a distraction from faith; it’s actually the foundation of it.
This way of looking at things even changes how we think about self-denial. It’s not about turning down happiness, but about searching for a deeper, more lasting joy. Sometimes that means letting go of smaller pleasures to experience something much greater. It’s like when someone swaps junk food for healthy meals—not out of guilt, but because they’ve discovered how good healthy living can feel. The sacrifice is real, but it’s driven by a desire for something better.
Now, a lot of people find it tough to accept that God wants to be glorified above everything else. It can sound a little self-centered or demanding, right? But when you realize that God’s glory and our happiness go hand in hand, everything shifts. God isn’t after glory at the cost of our joy—He’s actually inviting us into the fullness of joy that only He can offer. The more we delight in Him, the more His greatness shines through.
And here’s the best part: this truth brings real freedom. Faith stops feeling like grim determination or empty routine. It becomes a journey—one where you’re discovering the deepest joy imaginable, a joy that’s found in God alone. So, the search for happiness? Far from being a distraction, it’s actually the path to glorifying God.
